chunks.section: Spectral Rank and Step-Direction Dynamics in Language-Model Post-Training
chunks.text: Khurram Khalil khurram.khalil@missouri.edu Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering & Computer Science Affiliation: University of Missouri-Columbia, MO, USA Khaza Anuarul Hoque hoquek@missouri.edu Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering & Computer Science Affiliation: University of Missouri-Columbia, MO, USA

Understanding how language models change during post-training requires characterizing both the structure of cumulative weight updates and the directions of successive training displacements. Existing studies report seemingly contrasting spectral properties, including nearly full-rank updates and low stable-rank cumulative changes. We show that these observations are mathematically compatible and investigate how weight-update directions evolve during training. Language-model post-training changes a model’s behavior by changing its weights. Supervised fine-tuning ( sft ) learns from demonstration responses, while reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards ( rlvr ) learns from sampled responses scored by an automatic checker. Weight-space measurements describe how these procedures alter a pretrained model and inform methods that operate on weight differences, including task arithmetic and low-rank adaptation ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2022 ) . Interpreting those measurements requires separating the mathematical object being measured from the functional applied to it. That distinction matters when comparing recent accounts of post-training geometry. Mukherjee et al. (2025) report sparse, nearly full-algebraic-rank rlvr updates. Zhu et al. (2025) analyze update localization, numerical precision, and alignment with principal weight subspaces. Shen et al. (2026) compare cumulative updates in on-policy distillation, rlvr , and sft , reporting low stable rank for distillation and the rlvr endpoint. These studies characterize different aspects of adaptation. Yet their rank descriptions can appear incompatible if algebraic rank, stable rank, and energy coverage are treated as interchangeable. A comparison on the same update matrix is needed to determine what each description actually implies. We address this question with an explicit spectral construction and full-spectrum measurements of selected updates.

Even a complete endpoint spectrum leaves a second question unanswered. It does not determine whether consecutive training displacements reinforce or oppose one another. Analyses of full weight matrices ( He & Cao, 2025 ) and trajectory-level linear trends ( Wang et al., 2026 ) provide complementary information, but neither an endpoint change nor a fitted trend determines the inner products between consecutive finite displacements. We therefore measure direction at specified checkpoint widths and separations. These measurements describe local alignment on the saved checkpoint grid. Differences in trajectory alignment raise a third question. How does the advantage estimator affect the direction of weight updates under a shared training schedule? We investigate this question through a controlled comparison of group-relative advantages and a learned critic with generalized advantage estimation. Holding the actor schedule and sampled prompt stream fixed connects the observed geometry to a specific change in the training procedure. These investigations provide complementary views of post-training geometry. Spectral analysis characterizes how the cumulative weight change is distributed across singular directions, while trajectory analysis examines how successive weight changes interact during training. The controlled comparison then investigates whether changing the advantage system alters these directional relationships. Together, these measurements distinguish the structure of the final update from the geometry of the path taken to reach it.

Our contributions follow these three questions. First, we prove that low stable rank and large fixed-energy rank coexist for a family of power-law singular spectra, and verify the separation with full decompositions of OLMo-2-7B cumulative updates. Second, we document negative consecutive-displacement cosines across nine public rlvr stage trajectories, including ppo and grpo releases, quantify their temporal extent and opposing components, and test supervised alignment across four model families and two Llama precision settings. Third, we identify an advantage-system effect in six matched OLMo-2-1B runs. The critic–GAE arm reduces late-training alignment by 0.247 0.247 on average relative to the group-relative arm, with a paired seed-level 95 % 95\% interval of [ − 0.358 , − 0.137 ] [-0.358,-0.137] for the signed difference. Together, these contributions reconcile spectral descriptions of post-training and establish trajectory direction as a separately measurable aspect of adaptation.

Our public-release analysis covers nine rlvr stages in the OLMo-2, OLMoE, and Olmo-3 releases. Table 3 lists each stage and its native checkpoint width. The OLMo-2 stages include 7B and 13B ppo releases and 1B and 32B grpo releases. We report successive stages within each model lineage separately and retain their shared lineage in the checkpoint inventory. For sft , we analyze author-run trajectories from four model families on a uniform 500-optimizer-step grid through step 5,000. The comparison includes OLMo-2-7B and Llama-3.2-3B at seeds 42, 43, and 44, Mistral-7B-v0.3 at seeds 42 and 43, and Qwen2.5-3B at seed 42. Training stops at step 5,000 while preserving that schedule. The OLMo seed-42 run continues to step 29,356 and supplies the sft endpoint for spectral analysis. The cross-family runs store trainable parameters and Adam states in BF16. Two additional Llama runs at seeds 42 and 43 use FP32 parameters and Adam states with BF16 autocast, retaining the data mixture, effective batch size, learning-rate schedule, and measurement grid. chunks.section: 3.3 Exact directional measurements and spectral validation
chunks.text: Directional measurements accumulate full-parameter dot products and squared norms in FP64 over coordinate chunks, including normalization weights. For eight retained trajectories, we independently compute the displacement Gram matrix G i ​ j = ⟨ D i , D j ⟩ G_{ij}=\langle D_{i},D_{j}\rangle , which supplies both higher-separation correlations and norm-aware projections. Online and saved-checkpoint cosines for the six matched runs agree within 1.4 × 10 − 12 1.4\times 10^{-12} in absolute value. For the fourteen selected spectral cases, we compute a full FP64 singular decomposition. Reduced QR followed by full SVD preserves the complete singular spectrum of high-aspect-ratio matrices. Leading singular-triplet residuals are below 10 − 10 10^{-10} . We compare these results with the original randomized SVD configuration, ten oversamples and four power iterations ( Halko et al., 2011 ) , using seeds 42, 43, and 44, and a stronger setting with forty oversamples and eight iterations at seed 42. Rank-256 and rank-512 approximations are computed independently. We separate singular-value error from error introduced by the original FP32 norm and denominator regularizer. Energy-threshold reporting requires sufficient spectral accuracy. If an approximate top- K K energy remains below τ \tau , approximation error alone may explain the shortfall. Without a certified error bound, we label the threshold unresolved at the computed budget , not k τ > K k_{\tau}>K . All energy-threshold ranks used as quantitative evidence below come from full decompositions. Appendix F documents the corrected initialization and coordinate-sketch errors in the earlier analysis.

chunks.section: 4.1 Low stable rank coexists with large energy rank
chunks.text: Full decompositions verify the spectral separation on the same update matrices. Table 2 reports all fourteen cases, and Figure 1 shows representative cumulative energy curves. The three PPO query updates have stable ranks 9.58 9.58 , 18.14 18.14 , and 18.27 18.27 , while their 80 % 80\% -energy ranks are 532 532 , 1,222 1{,}222 , and 1,149 1{,}149 . These matrices combine strong leading-value concentration with an energetic tail spanning hundreds of components. The same distinction applies to the MLP updates. The selected PPO down projection at layer 16 has stable rank 58.78 58.78 but k 0.8 = 2,120 k_{0.8}=2{,}120 . Its sft counterpart has stable rank 792.32 792.32 and k 0.8 = 2,250 k_{0.8}=2{,}250 . The stable ranks differ by more than an order of magnitude while their energy ranks are close. Conversely, the sft query update at layer 0 has k 0.8 = 1 k_{0.8}=1 . The two functionals thus reveal different aspects of variation across matrices, with stable rank distinguishing concentration even when energy ranks are similar. These observations reconcile the logical content of the prior rank descriptions. Near-full algebraic rank permits a dominant leading singular value, and a dominant leading value permits a long energetic tail. Proposition 1 supplies an explicit family with this behavior. Thus, low stable rank alone does not generally imply that a small number of singular components captures most of the update energy.

chunks.section: 4.3 A controlled effect on alignment magnitude
chunks.text: The effect persists in the secondary matched-width summaries. At widths 10, 20, and 40, all paired late-training differences are negative (Appendix C ). Their magnitudes change with width, illustrating why equal aggregation units matter. The group-relative seed mean increases from 0.071 0.071 at width 10 to 0.259 0.259 at width 60. Matching aggregation width makes the measured advantage-system effect interpretable at a shared response and optimizer-update budget. Training-health checks accompany the geometry measurements. The runs record realized response lengths, EOS completion, and finite updates. Training cap-hit fractions range from 0.213 % 0.213\% to 1.189 % 1.189\% . Randomized SVD supports efficient broad scans, while these functional-specific errors motivate full decompositions for the reported energy ranks and subspace angles. These findings highlight the importance of validating numerical approximations against the specific spectral or geometric quantity being reported.

The spectral and trajectory results describe complementary aspects of adaptation. Stable rank measures concentration around the leading singular value, while energy-threshold rank measures the breadth of the spectrum needed to retain a specified energy fraction. Consecutive-displacement cosine adds information about how successive changes interact. The public trajectories show anti-alignment across several RLVR recipes, and the controlled study demonstrates that the advantage system affects alignment magnitude under a shared actor schedule. The rank reconciliation explains how the reported spectral descriptions coexist. The power-law construction establishes this compatibility analytically, and the full decompositions demonstrate it on selected updates. Its practical implication is that a small stable rank can accompany substantial energy outside a low-rank approximation. Assessing the task-level value of that energy requires evaluating models after spectral truncation. The public survey measures aggregated changes on each release’s native checkpoint grid. Differences in schedules, exposure budgets, storage precision, and related stages limit causal comparisons across releases. The supervised study spans four model families under one data mixture and schedule, with the FP32 follow-up covering two Llama seeds. Its negative Mistral and FP32 Llama pairs show why trajectory sign should be interpreted together with the model and numerical training configuration. The controlled RL study covers one 1B initialization, one task source, one shared trainer, and three paired seeds. Its seed-level intervals characterize variation within that setting.

The controlled intervention combines critic fitting, GAE, and advantage normalization, so its effect applies to that package. Generated-token exposure remains policy-dependent, and the small held-out diagnostic shows no consistent performance improvement. Both local arms have higher mean alignment than the public RLVR trajectories. Identifying the source of this difference requires interventions within the production implementation, with matched exposure and adequate task evaluation. Full-SVD validation covers fourteen matrices selected by shape and layer position. The resulting accuracy measurements apply to this sample. All geometric quantities describe stored checkpoint weights, whose numerical precision affects apparent support sparsity and small displacements.

In this work, we studied language-model post-training by separating the structure of cumulative weight updates from the directions of successive training displacements. Our power-law construction showed that low stable rank and large fixed-energy rank are mathematically compatible, and full decompositions verified this separation in selected OLMo-2-7B updates. A dominant singular value can therefore coexist with hundreds of components needed to retain most of an update’s energy. This distinction clarifies why different rank measures can give contrasting descriptions of the same matrix. Trajectory measurements add information about how successive weight changes interact. All 131 measured adjacent pairs across nine public RLVR stages from the OLMo-2, OLMoE, and Olmo-3 releases had negative cosine on their native checkpoint grids, including PPO and GRPO releases. Supervised comparisons of OLMo-2-7B, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Mistral-7B-v0.3 showed configuration-dependent alignment, with late anti-alignment in Mistral and FP32 Llama runs.
